accepted.reason: Python's default inventory retries this part with local degradation (its strict hole evidence refuses on a solid BRepCheck calls invalid), and the retried run skips this record; `features::recognise` takes the retry only where its own strict hole evidence refuses, which on this part it does not (captured/local_degradation/known.json, retry), so it publishes it. Python skips the fillet because it touches the bad-face region of a solid OpenCascade's BRepCheck calls unorientable after its import healing re-orients wires; the file's own topology is closed and consistently oriented and the port accepts the solid, so publishing it is right (captured/local_degradation/known.json's two cgb202 fillet skips and this file's recognise_fillets evidence entry in known_divergences.json, rust-correct).

Not a reconciliation difference: the same hole's candidate defining faces differ. Python's hole claims the internal-groove cylinder it calls a spotface (with its faces) because it orders segments by their high end in either drilling direction; the port orders by the end nearest the opening, finds no spotface and claims the bore alone. Python's public recognise_holes gives the same faces as its aggregate candidate (corpus.json). See this file's recognise_holes spotface entry in known_divergences.json (rust-correct).

Not a reconciliation difference: the same through hole's candidate defining faces differ with its drilling end. Python drills this Ø22 hole from the Ø102 end (it takes whichever segment comes first in face order at the Ø110 end, where the bore and the Ø110 segment end level), its counterbore the Ø102 one; the port drills from the wider Ø110 end, as Python's own rule says and as Python does with the part turned over, so the segments each side claims with the bore differ. Python's public recognise_holes gives the same faces as its aggregate candidate (corpus.json). See this file's recognise_holes axis/cbore entry in known_divergences.json (rust-correct).

Not a reconciliation difference: the same hole's candidate defining faces differ. Python's hole claims the Ø61.62 cylinder 0.47 mm inside the mouth it calls a spotface (with its faces) because it orders segments by their high end in either drilling direction; the port orders by the end nearest the opening, finds no spotface and claims the bore alone. Python's public recognise_holes gives the same faces as its aggregate candidate (corpus.json). See this file's recognise_holes spotface entry in known_divergences.json (rust-correct).

Not a reconciliation difference: Python's aggregate discovers plates only on solids that own no turned step (plates.py _discover passes the turned steps' solids as excluded_solids), and this part's one solid owns its turned steps (its four bosses are rejected as exactly turned steps). The port's plates::discover has no such exclusion, so the aggregate's plate dependency on turned steps is not ported.

The same slot face lists are retained in a stable order. Raw centres still measure the geometry; only the width/centre ordering key is quantised to six decimal places with the kernel coordinate floor. Infinitesimal differences in a tied centre coordinate must not override the next distinct coordinate or exchange section-recess indices. recess_reduce::tests and the generic-framed NIST FTC 06/10 document checks independently establish this ordering correction; the frozen Python ordering is not authoritative.

All 30 holes and seven patterns remain accepted. Four symmetric diameter-7 length-55 through bores have equal diameter-10 length-10 mouths at both ends (independent OpenCascade). Their one-sided counterbore attribution is unproved, so Rust claims the bore faces [146],[147],[148],[149] and retains an end gauge, while Python arbitrarily claims one mouth as well. The symmetric-double-mouth motion control checks that the feature is retained.
